headline: Navigation is finding your way through space—using Earth's hidden signals to know where you are
universal_truth: Orientation requires reference points; you can only know where you are relative to something else
fun_facts: Compasses point to magnetic north, which is not the same as 'true' north—and it moves over time
Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open ocean using stars, waves, and bird patterns
GPS works by calculating your position from signals from at least four satellites
discussion_questions: How would you navigate without technology?
What happens to our navigation skills when we rely entirely on GPS?
How do you find your way in unfamiliar places?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: You're in unfamiliar territory. Which way is home? Humans have answered this question using stars, sun shadows, magnetic rocks, and now satellites. Navigation is the art of knowing where you are—using signals the Earth and sky provide.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Before GPS, how did people navigate across oceans with no landmarks? How can you know your position in the middle of an empty sea?
cliff.prompt: How did ancient navigators cross open oceans?

options.text: They used celestial bodies, wave patterns, wind direction, and bird behavior as reference points
options.response: Yes. Stars give direction, wave patterns indicate land, birds fly from shore. The environment provides subtle signals.

options.text: They followed coastlines and never went out of sight of land
options.response: Coastal navigation was common, but Polynesians crossed thousands of miles of open ocean...

q1.title: The Magnetic Mystery
q1.script: Compasses work because Earth has a magnetic field—like a giant magnet with poles. But magnetic north isn't true north; it's offset by degrees that vary by location. And magnetic north moves—it's currently drifting toward Siberia.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "The Magnetic Mystery"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Polynesian Masters
q2.script: Polynesian navigators crossed the Pacific—2,500 miles of open ocean—using no instruments. They read star positions, wave patterns, ocean swells, and bird behavior. Their mental maps of the sea were remarkably accurate.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Satellite Position
q3.script: GPS calculates your position by timing signals from multiple satellites. Each satellite broadcasts its location and time; your device calculates distance from timing differences. Four satellites pinpoint you anywhere on Earth.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Orientation requires reference points. You can only know where you are relative to something else. Navigation teaches that position is always relational—true for physical space and for life.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 107. Tomorrow, we'll go deeper into finding your way. Until then, notice how you navigate—what reference points do you use to know where you are?
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Navigation Without GPS - Find Your Bearings
growTrack.learning_objective: Develop awareness of natural navigation cues
growTrack.activity: Today, turn off GPS for a short trip you know. Navigate by landmarks, sun position, or memory. What do you notice when you can't rely on technology? What natural cues are you ignoring when GPS does the work?
